criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — DELIBERATE PROPORTIONS & SCALING. Body proportions are a CHOSEN, role-readable decision driven by HumanoidDescription's scale axes (BodyTypeScale / HeightScale / WidthScale / HeadScale / ProportionScale) and anchored to a named proportion archetype (Classic ~4.75 studs blocky; Rthro Normal ~5.75-6.5, wider shoulders/narrow hips; Rthro Slender ~5.25-6.25, narrow shoulders/wider hips — with the matching AvatarPartScaleType), tuned so the silhouette reads the intended body language (hero / grunt / heavy / lithe / creature) at a glance — NOT the default stock R15 proportions left on every character. The discriminator is whether the build commits to a deliberate per-archetype proportion choice expressed through the named scale axes: passing requires (1) a stated archetype/body-language target AND (2) specific HumanoidDescription scale-axis values (or per-region segment scaling) set to hit it, applied via ApplyDescription / LoadCharacterWithHumanoidDescription, with exaggeration deliberate and per-region rather than a uniform stretch (and any deviation from humanoid proportion landmarks — e.g. hands resting slightly below the hips, torso not as tall as the legs — chosen knowingly). A build that ships the default R15 body with no deliberate proportion choice (or sets a single Color/shirt but never touches scale) FAILS. A build that names an archetype AND sets the scale axes to a distinctive role-readable silhouette PASSES; multiple contrasting archetypes in one cast (hero vs heavy vs grunt) and documented intentional landmark deviations push toward full marks. A build that nudges one scale axis with no archetype intent, or uniformly scales the whole body, earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: The single biggest tell of a generic/AI character is the stock R15 body with default proportions on everyone — proportion is framed across the docs as the FIRST identity decision, and the five named HumanoidDescription scale axes plus the archetype stud-height/shoulder-hip ratios are exactly what make a character read 'heroic/bulky' vs 'lithe/agile' before any texture. Per-region deliberate exaggeration (not a uniform stretch, which DevForum reviewers flag as 'the whole thing looks wrong') and respecting/knowingly-breaking proportion landmarks is what reads as style rather than a mistake. Grading the archetype-PLUS-scale-axis commitment keeps it discriminating: a deliberately-scaled archetype clears it; the default body cannot. Note R15-only — scales don't affect R6.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing (1) a named proportion archetype / body-language target (hero/grunt/heavy/lithe/creature; Classic/Rthro Normal/Slender) AND (2) specific HumanoidDescription scale-axis values (BodyTypeScale/HeightScale/WidthScale/HeadScale/ProportionScale) or per-region segment scaling set to achieve it, applied via Humanoid:ApplyDescription / LoadCharacterWithHumanoidDescription, with deliberate per-region (not uniform) exaggeration and any landmark deviation stated as intentional. Multiple contrasting archetypes in one cast earn full marks. The default R15 body with no scale choice, or only a Color/shirt swap, does NOT satisfy this; one nudged axis with no archetype intent, or a uniform whole-body stretch, earns partial.

grading.pass: Names a proportion archetype/body-language target AND sets specific HumanoidDescription scale-axis values (or per-region segment scaling) to hit it, applied via ApplyDescription/LoadCharacterWithHumanoidDescription, with deliberate per-region exaggeration; full marks for multiple contrasting archetypes in one cast plus documented intentional landmark deviations.
grading.partial: Nudges one scale axis with no archetype intent, or uniformly scales the whole body (a stretch rather than a per-region role-readable proportion choice).
grading.fail: Ships the default R15 body with no deliberate proportion choice, or sets only a Color/shirt and never touches scale.

criteria.concrete_fix: Pick the archetype and body language first (e.g. heavy = Rthro Normal, high WidthScale/BodyTypeScale, larger HeadScale for readability), then set the HumanoidDescription scale axes to hit it and apply via ApplyDescription; exaggerate per-region (torso/neck/limbs individually against a reference) rather than scaling the whole body, and check it against the humanoid landmarks (hands slightly below hips, torso shorter than legs) — deviating only on purpose.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — COHESIVE THEMED OUTFIT. Accessories and clothing are composed into ONE unified, theme-coherent character identity — a curated set with consistent shape language and a single era/faction/theme spine — deliberately MIXING accessory classes (deformable layered clothing + RIGID hardpoint accessories like helmet/backpack/pauldrons + optional custom hands/feet meshes) with restraint, rather than a random unthemed pile of marketplace hats. The discriminator is whether the build commits to a theme-driven, multi-class, restrained composition placed on the correct anchors: passing requires (1) a stated theme/era/faction spine that every piece serves (consistent shape language), AND (2) a deliberate composition of at least two accessory classes — layered (cage-driven) clothing for body-conforming coverage PLUS rigid hardpoint pieces for structural silhouette shapes — placed on the correct standardized attachment points with awareness of their behavior (e.g. shoulder attachments move with the arm, collar attachments do not; using Head/Neck/Shoulder/Front/Back offset adjustments) and a budgeted count that keeps the silhouette uncluttered (kawaii = solid clothing + 1-2 accent accessories, not a 100+ item pile). A build that is an unthemed pile of random catalog hats, or a single flat classic shirt/pants with no composition, FAILS. A build that composes a theme-coherent rigid+layered outfit with restrained count on correct anchors PASSES; non-clipping centered placement via the adjustment APIs and rigid-for-shape / layered-for-conform role separation push toward full marks. A build with a theme but only one accessory class (e.g. all flat clothing, or one accessory) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic avatars are either an all-flat classic shirt/pants or a random pile of unthemed marketplace hats — clipping, off-center, over-piled — with no governing theme. A deliberately composed outfit that mixes RIGID structural pieces (for crisp silhouette shapes) with DEFORMABLE layered clothing (for body-conforming cloth), bound by one theme/era/faction spine and restrained in count, is what produces a game-character-grade identity rather than asset-store soup. Knowing the 19 standardized attachment points and that collar-vs-shoulder anchors animate differently is what keeps the composition reading correctly in motion instead of floating/clipping. Grading the theme-PLUS-multi-class-PLUS-restraint commitment keeps it discriminating: a composed themed outfit clears it; an unthemed hat-pile cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing (1) a theme/era/faction spine with consistent shape language that every piece serves, AND (2) a deliberate mix of >=2 accessory classes — layered (cage-driven) clothing PLUS rigid hardpoint accessories (helmet/backpack/pauldrons) — placed on correct standardized attachment points (Hat/Hair/Face/Neck/Shoulder/Collar/Back/Front/Waist, with shoulder-moves-with-arm vs collar-does-not awareness) and a restrained, non-clipping count. Centered placement via the Accessory Adjustment APIs and rigid-for-shape/layered-for-conform role separation earn full marks. A random unthemed hat-pile, or a single flat shirt/pants, does NOT satisfy this; a theme with only one accessory class earns partial.

grading.pass: States a theme/era/faction spine every piece serves AND composes >=2 accessory classes (layered clothing PLUS rigid hardpoint pieces) on correct standardized attachment points with restrained, non-clipping count; full marks for centered placement via the Accessory Adjustment APIs and explicit rigid-for-shape/layered-for-conform role separation.
grading.partial: Has a theme but uses only one accessory class (e.g. all flat clothing, or a single accessory).
grading.fail: An unthemed pile of random catalog hats, or a single flat classic shirt/pants with no composition.

criteria.concrete_fix: Pick one theme/era/faction spine, then compose the outfit from both classes: layered clothing for body-conforming coverage and rigid accessories (helmet, pauldrons, backpack) for structural silhouette shapes; place each on the correct attachment (shoulder pauldron on the shoulder attachment so it follows the arm, a cape on the collar so it does not), center them with the Head/Neck/Shoulder/Front/Back adjustment offsets, and budget the count so the silhouette stays uncluttered.

criteria.statement: CUSTOM-BODY COMMITMENT vs STOCK BODY. The build commits to a CUSTOM character body — custom MeshPart limbs/heads or a non-humanoid creature body authored to be rigged and animated (Motor6D-jointed, skin-weighted, no clipping/gaps at the joints) — rather than shipping the stock blocky R15 body with zero authored geometry. The discriminator is binary at the floor: does the build author its own body geometry at all, and is that geometry declared as riggable and non-clipping (so clothing/accessories can anchor and the mesh animates cleanly)? Passing requires a stated custom MeshPart body or creature rig with (1) Motor6D joints on animated parts (weld on static) and skin weighting, AND (2) a no-clipping / no-gaps-at-joints commitment. A build that ships the stock R15 body with no custom meshes FAILS (there is no authored body to hold to a structural contract). A build that names custom MeshPart limbs/creature rigs with weighting + no-clipping intent PASSES; adding the explicit avatar structural contract (15 MeshParts / R15 16-bone skeleton / WrapTarget cages / 19 Attachments / catalog-compatible traced topology) and mesh hygiene (sealed watertight openings, checked normals, deformation loop-cuts, averaged seam normals) pushes toward full marks. A build that asserts custom geometry but gives neither the weighting/Motor6D nor the no-clipping commitment earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: The single biggest tell separating a designed character from the generic default is whether ANY custom body geometry exists — the stock R15 body is what you get by not designing the character. Custom MeshPart limbs/creature rigs that are weighted, Motor6D-jointed, and non-clipping are the foundation the look/identity layers compose on; the full structural contract and hygiene steps are the depth that takes a custom body from 'authored' to 'ships clean.' Grading the custom-body-with-riggable-non-clipping-intent floor keeps it discriminating: a build that authors a riggable custom body clears it; the stock default cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement that the body is CUSTOM geometry (custom MeshPart limbs/heads or a non-humanoid creature rig), with (1) Motor6D joints on animated parts (welds on static) and skin weighting AND (2) a no-clipping / no-gaps-at-joints commitment. The avatar structural contract (15 MeshParts / R15 16-bone skeleton / WrapTarget cages / 19 Attachments / catalog-compatible traced topology) and mesh hygiene (sealed openings, checked normals, deformation loop-cuts, averaged seams) earn full marks. The stock R15 body with no custom meshes does NOT satisfy this; custom geometry asserted without the weighting/Motor6D or the no-clipping commitment earns partial.

grading.pass: Commits to a CUSTOM body (custom MeshPart limbs/heads or non-humanoid creature rig) with Motor6D-on-animated/weld-on-static + skin weighting AND a no-clipping/no-gaps-at-joints commitment; full marks for the explicit structural contract (15 MeshParts / R15 16-bone skeleton / WrapTarget cages / 19 Attachments / catalog-compatible traced topology) plus mesh hygiene (sealed openings, checked normals, deformation loop-cuts, averaged seam normals).
grading.partial: Asserts custom body geometry but supplies neither the Motor6D/weighting nor the no-clipping/no-gaps commitment.
grading.fail: Ships the stock R15 body with no custom meshes (no authored body to hold to a structural contract).

criteria.concrete_fix: Author the body as custom geometry instead of using the stock R15 default: give each animated part a Motor6D joint (weld static parts), skin-weight it, and commit to no clipping/gaps at the joints; then take it to full marks by holding to the avatar structural contract (trace the stock rig to keep 15 MeshParts / 16 bones / WrapTarget cages / 19 attachments so catalog clothing still fits) and cleaning topology (seal openings, check normals, add deformation loop-cuts, average seam normals).
criteria.change_reason: Original keyed PASS on a full structural-contract dump (15 MeshParts / 16 bones / WrapTarget cages / 19 attachments / watertight hygiene) that NEITHER artifact provides, so the great failed alongside the mean (no separation). The great artifact does commit to 'custom MeshPart limbs or non-humanoid creature rigs (Motor6D, weighted, no clipping)'; the mean ships the stock body with 'no custom meshes.' Re-anchoring the floor on 'authors a riggable, non-clipping custom body at all' lets the great clear the bar on its actual evidence while the stock default fails outright; the contract/hygiene specifics are demoted from the pass gate to the full-marks band so the criterion still rewards depth without requiring evidence the great lacks.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM (color half) — DESIGNED COLOR PALETTE. The character uses a constrained, harmonized color palette (typically 3-5 colors, often 2-3 for a skin) with a clear value/weight hierarchy — a ~60% dominant color, ~30% secondary, and a small deliberate accent placed as the single focal point — using analogous/complementary relationships rather than random equal-weight catalog colors. The discriminator is whether the build commits to a designed palette with hierarchy AND validates its value structure: passing requires (1) a limited palette (3-5 primary colors) with a dominant/secondary/accent weighting (60/30/10-style) and a named harmony relationship (analogous or complementary), NOT random saturated equal-weight colors, AND (2) a value/contrast check — the palette locked/verified at low saturation (e.g. desaturate to ~25% under multiple lighting conditions) so forms don't merge and the accent still reads as the focal point. A build using default gray, or random saturated equal-weight colors with no focal point, FAILS. A build that states a limited dominant/secondary/accent palette AND a value-structure/desaturation check PASSES; locking a left-to-right color-script strip before texturing and checking under multiple lighting setups push toward full marks. A build with a limited palette but no value/contrast check (or a value check but no deliberate accent/hierarchy) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic avatars use random equal-weight catalog colors with no hierarchy — visual noise with no focal point, or default gray — and chase hue while ignoring value, so they read muddy and merge with the environment. A deliberate dominant/secondary/accent ratio with one intentional accent gives the eye a place to land, and the desaturate-and-check test guarantees the character holds up in VALUE (not just hue) at distance and in crowded scenes. This palette-discipline-PLUS-value-test is what reads as 'art-directed' rather than 'colors thrown at it.' Grading both halves keeps it discriminating: a hierarchized, value-validated palette clears it; a random-saturated default cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing (1) a limited palette (3-5 colors, 2-3 for a skin) with a dominant/secondary/accent weighting (~60/30/10) and a named analogous/complementary harmony, NOT random equal-weight or default colors, AND (2) a value/contrast validation — desaturate to low saturation under multiple lighting conditions, confirm forms don't merge and the accent reads as focal. A pre-locked color-script strip and multi-lighting check earn full marks. Default gray or random saturated equal-weight colors with no focal point do NOT satisfy this; a limited palette with no value check, or a value check with no accent/hierarchy, earns partial.

grading.pass: States a limited palette (3-5 colors) with dominant/secondary/accent ~60/30/10 weighting and a named analogous/complementary harmony AND a value/contrast validation (desaturate under multiple lighting conditions, forms stay separated, accent reads focal); full marks for a pre-locked color-script strip and multi-lighting check.
grading.partial: Has a limited palette but no value/contrast check, OR a value check but no deliberate accent/hierarchy.
grading.fail: Uses default gray, or random saturated equal-weight colors with no focal point.

criteria.concrete_fix: Lock a limited palette before texturing: one dominant color over ~60% of the character, ~30% secondary in a nearby hue, and a single complementary accent for the focal point; then desaturate the character to ~25% under front/side/rim lighting and confirm forms stay separated and the accent still pops — adjust values until they do.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM (material half) — INTENTIONAL PBR MATERIALS. Different surfaces read as different physical materials via a deliberate per-region material hierarchy — metal vs rough cloth/canvas vs skin — using SurfaceAppearance with the four PBR maps (ColorMap/albedo, NormalMap, MetalnessMap, RoughnessMap) and/or per-region Material+Reflectance choices, with values based on the real-world material and tested across varied lighting — NOT the default flat plastic look on the whole body. The discriminator is whether the build commits to material CONTRAST grounded in physically-based values: passing requires (1) at least two distinct material reads on one character (e.g. metallic bands vs canvas/fabric vs skin) set via SurfaceAppearance maps or per-region Material/Reflectance, AND (2) physically-based value discipline — MetalnessMap near 0.0 (non-metal) or 1.0 (metal) with intermediate grays only for weathering, RoughnessMap as a deliberate gloss-to-matte value (glossy 0 to matte 1, ~0.1 rougher to compensate Fresnel), an OpenGL-tangent-space NormalMap, single-atlas/one-material-per-mesh — chosen from the real material and verified across lighting environments, not tuned to look good in one scene. A build that leaves the default uniform Plastic material (metalness/roughness defaults) on the whole body FAILS. A build that commits to >=2 physically-based material reads with correct metalness/roughness discipline PASSES; a NormalMap adding close-range micro-detail, AlphaMode chosen per region (Overlay to keep recolorability, Transparency for crisp cutouts/skin show-through), and multi-lighting verification push toward full marks. A build that varies material per region but with non-physical/arbitrary metalness-roughness values (or one PBR material but no contrast) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Uniform default Plastic on every part (metalness 0 / roughness 0, environment-tuned to one scene) is the #1 material tell of a generic Roblox character. Per-region material contrast (metal vs canvas vs skin) with physically-based binary-metalness / value-gradient-roughness / OpenGL-normal discipline and cross-lighting testing is exactly what gives materials a grounded, non-AI read across the game's varied lighting, and the single-atlas/one-material-per-mesh + correct-normal-convention specifics are engine-correctness gates generic work gets wrong (a flipped normal G-channel inverts bumps). Grading the contrast-PLUS-physical-values commitment keeps it discriminating: a physically-grounded multi-material character clears it; a uniform-plastic body cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing (1) >=2 distinct material reads on one character (metal vs rough cloth/canvas vs skin) via SurfaceAppearance maps or per-region Material/Reflectance, AND (2) physically-based discipline — MetalnessMap ~0 or ~1 (grays only for weathering), RoughnessMap as a gloss-to-matte value, OpenGL-tangent NormalMap, single-atlas/one-material-per-mesh — based on the real material and tested across lighting environments. NormalMap micro-detail, per-region AlphaMode (Overlay vs Transparency), and multi-lighting verification earn full marks. Default uniform Plastic over the whole body does NOT satisfy this; per-region variation with non-physical metalness/roughness values, or one PBR material with no contrast, earns partial.

grading.pass: Commits to >=2 distinct physically-based material reads on one character (metal vs cloth/canvas vs skin via SurfaceAppearance maps or per-region Material/Reflectance) with correct metalness (~0 or ~1) / roughness (gloss-to-matte) / OpenGL-normal / single-atlas discipline, real-material-based and cross-lighting-tested; full marks for NormalMap micro-detail, per-region AlphaMode, and multi-lighting verification.
grading.partial: Varies material per region but with non-physical/arbitrary metalness-roughness values, OR uses one PBR material but no material contrast.
grading.fail: Leaves the default uniform Plastic material (metalness/roughness defaults) on the whole body.

criteria.concrete_fix: Author a material hierarchy: give metal regions a SurfaceAppearance with MetalnessMap ~1.0 and a low RoughnessMap, fabric/canvas regions metalness 0 and a high roughness, skin its own map — all baked into one atlas per mesh with an OpenGL-tangent NormalMap for close-range bumps — set values from the real material and check the character under several lighting environments rather than tuning to one scene.

criteria.statement: AUTHORED LAYERED CLOTHING vs NO CLOTHING / FLAT DECAL. Clothing is AUTHORED layered (WrapLayer/cage-driven) garments composed into the outfit so cloth conforms to the body and stretches over any scale — rather than no clothing at all, or a single flat classic shirt/pants decal painted on the stock body. The discriminator at the floor is whether deformable layered clothing is authored and composed onto the character: passing requires (1) at least one stated layered (WrapLayer cage-driven) garment that conforms to the body (not a flat 2D shirt/pants decal), composed as part of the outfit identity, AND (2) a fit/no-clip commitment (the garment stretches over the body scale without clipping). A build with no clothing, or only a flat classic shirt/pants decal, FAILS. A build that authors layered cage-driven clothing composed onto the character with a fit/no-clip commitment PASSES; the full inner/outer cage discipline (inner cage controlling fit tightness, outer cage snapped just outside along normals enabling Hidden Surface Removal) plus cage hygiene (even edge-loop spacing, never-delete-verts, rigid bits left outside the cage, cage kept tight) pushes toward full marks. A build that names layered clothing but states neither the conform-to-body nor the no-clip/fit behavior earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic clothing is a flat decal shirt or no clothing at all; authored layered (WrapLayer) garments that actually conform to the body and stretch over any scale are what give a character real cloth and a composed outfit identity. The inner/outer cage discipline and HSR are the depth that make multi-layer outfits compose cleanly across the avatar ecosystem. Grading the authored-layered-clothing-with-fit floor keeps it discriminating: a build that authors conforming layered clothing clears it; a flat decal or bare stock body cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement that the outfit includes at least one AUTHORED layered (WrapLayer cage-driven) garment conforming to the body (not a flat 2D shirt/pants decal), composed into the character identity, with a fit/no-clip commitment (stretches over body scale without clipping). The full inner/outer cage discipline (inner controls fit, outer snapped just outside along normals, HSR) plus cage hygiene (even edge-loops, never-delete-verts, rigid bits outside the cage, cage kept tight) earn full marks. No clothing, or a flat classic shirt/pants decal, does NOT satisfy this; layered clothing named without any conform/no-clip behavior earns partial.

grading.pass: Authors at least one layered (WrapLayer cage-driven) garment that conforms to the body and is composed into the outfit identity, with a fit/no-clip commitment; full marks for inner/outer cage discipline (inner-controls-fit, outer-just-outside-along-normals, HSR) plus cage hygiene (even edge-loops, never-delete-verts, rigid bits outside the cage, cage kept tight).
grading.partial: Names layered clothing but states neither the conform-to-body nor the no-clip/fit behavior.
grading.fail: No clothing at all, or only a flat classic shirt/pants decal on the stock body.

criteria.concrete_fix: Author the garment as layered (WrapLayer) clothing modeled on the body cage so it conforms and stretches over any scale, and compose it into the outfit identity with a no-clip commitment; then take it to full marks with proper cage discipline — model on the cage-as-mannequin, set the inner cage to control fit tightness, snap the outer cage just outside along normals so HSR culls interpenetration, keep edge loops even, never delete cage verts (hide them), and leave rigid spikes/pauldrons outside the cage.
criteria.change_reason: Original keyed PASS (and even partial) on an inner/outer cage-mechanism dump (inner-controls-fit / outer-just-outside-along-normals / HSR / cage hygiene) that the great artifact does not provide, so the great failed alongside the mean (no separation). The great commits to 'layered-clothing outfit composition forming one identity'; the mean has no clothing whatsoever. Re-anchoring the floor on 'authors deformable layered (WrapLayer) clothing composed onto the character, with a conform/no-clip commitment' lets the great clear the bar while no-clothing/flat-decal fails; the cage-authoring mechanics move to the full-marks band.

criteria.statement: CUSTOM RIG/MESH COMMITMENT vs STOCK-AVATAR DEFAULT. Where the design's identity calls for non-stock geometry, the build commits to custom MeshPart limbs/heads or a non-humanoid creature rig (Motor6D-jointed, skin-weighted, no clipping at joints, distinct per-part shapes) instead of leaving every character on the stock blocky humanoid. The discriminator removes the old stock-is-partial-by-default escape: a stock-avatar build for a cast that reads as generic/undesigned FAILS, because no custom geometry is the default-avatar failure mode this criterion exists to catch. Passing requires a stated custom MeshPart body or creature rig with (1) Motor6D on animated parts (weld on static) and skin weighting, AND (2) clean deformation intent — no clipping/gaps at joints and distinct per-part shapes (not one merged blob). A pure stock-avatar build with no custom geometry FAILS. A build that commits to custom MeshPart limbs/creature rigs (Motor6D, weighted, no clipping) where the design needs them PASSES; structurally-correct rig detail (economical joints concentrated in expressive appendages, neutral-pose modeling, pivots at real hinges, named Head + forward-facing PrimaryPart, tuned HipHeight, <=4 joints per vertex, or a Custom Bone/AnimationController rig with translation-based squash/stretch) pushes toward full marks. A build that gestures at custom rigs conditionally but commits neither the Motor6D/weighting nor the no-clip/distinct-shape deformation earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic character creation only ever uses the stock R15 humanoid, so any non-stock identity is impossible without custom geometry. The original's stock-is-partial-by-default rule let the most generic possible artifact bank partial credit, defeating the criterion's purpose. Treating the undesigned stock default as a FAIL and rewarding a committed custom Motor6D/weighted/no-clip rig (with rig-structure detail for full marks) is what restores separation between a designed creature/limb identity and the default avatar.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement committing to custom MeshPart limbs/heads or a non-humanoid creature rig where the design needs it, with (1) Motor6D on animated parts (weld on static) and skin weighting AND (2) clean deformation intent (no clipping/gaps at joints, distinct per-part shapes). Structurally-correct rig detail (economical joints concentrated in expressive appendages, neutral-pose modeling, pivots at real hinges, named Head + forward-facing PrimaryPart, tuned HipHeight, <=4 joints/vertex, or a Custom Bone/AnimationController rig with translation-based squash/stretch) earns full marks. A pure stock-avatar build with no custom geometry does NOT satisfy this; custom rigs gestured at without the Motor6D/weighting or the no-clip/distinct-shape commitment earns partial.

grading.pass: Commits to custom MeshPart limbs/heads or a non-humanoid creature rig where the design needs it, with Motor6D-on-animated/weld-on-static + skin weighting AND clean deformation (no clipping/gaps, distinct per-part shapes); full marks for structurally-correct rig detail (economical appendage-concentrated joints, neutral-pose modeling, pivots at real hinges, named Head + forward-facing PrimaryPart, tuned HipHeight, <=4 joints/vertex, or a Custom Bone/AnimationController rig with translation-based squash/stretch).
grading.partial: Gestures at custom rigs conditionally but commits neither the Motor6D/weighting nor the no-clip/distinct-per-part-shape deformation.
grading.fail: A pure stock-avatar build with no custom geometry (the undesigned default — no longer earns partial by default).

criteria.concrete_fix: For any identity the stock humanoid can't express, author a custom rig: give each animated part a Motor6D joint with skin weighting (weld static parts), commit to no clipping/gaps and distinct per-part shapes; then push to full marks with correct rig structure — model in a neutral pose, drag pivots to real hinges, name one part Head, add a forward-facing PrimaryPart, tune HipHeight, concentrate joints in expressive appendages, cap vertex weights at <=4, and for skinned creatures use a Custom Bone rig with translation-based squash/stretch.
criteria.change_reason: Both artifacts scored PARTIAL because the original granted 'a pure stock-avatar build earns partial credit by default' — so the mean (a stock default with NO design intent) was guaranteed partial and could never score below the great. That default partial is the exact escape hatch that broke discrimination. Removing it makes the undesigned stock-default cast a FAIL, while the great's actual commitment ('custom MeshPart limbs or non-humanoid creature rigs (Motor6D, weighted, no clipping) where the design needs them') clears a PASS. The structurally-correct-rig depth is demoted to the full-marks band so the criterion still rewards real rig fidelity.

criteria.statement: KILLER SYSTEM — VARIATION SYSTEM. Customization/variation is driven as a SYSTEM by HumanoidDescription applied via Humanoid:ApplyDescription / LoadCharacterWithHumanoidDescription — one description object carrying the full identity payload (scales + BodyColors + Shirt/Pants/ShirtGraphic + rigid SetAccessories + layered WrapTarget/WrapLayer accessories + body-part mesh IDs + face) used to produce skin/palette/accessory swaps for player choice or NPC crowd variety — NOT one hardcoded look duplicated on every character. The discriminator is whether the build commits to a data-driven variation system rather than per-character hand-built one-offs: passing requires (1) HumanoidDescription as the single identity payload (the full identity assembled in ONE description — scales/colors/accessories/clothing/face — built from a UserId/OutfitId then mutated, or composed from scratch) AND (2) APPLIED to drive variation — multiple distinct looks generated from the system (NPC crowd variety, randomized populations, or player-choice swaps) via ApplyDescription, not a single hardcoded appearance set part-by-part on every character. A build that hardcodes one look (sets a Color/shirt directly, the same on every character) FAILS. A build that drives skin/palette/accessory variation through ApplyDescription from a HumanoidDescription system PASSES; reusable skin-tone handling (texture opacity x MeshPart.Color or SurfaceAppearance Overlay AlphaMode, verified across several skin tones) and runtime per-part variation (AvatarCreationService + EditableImage/EditableMesh preserving skinning/FACS) push toward full marks. A build that uses a HumanoidDescription but only ever applies ONE look (no variation) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic player-customization is a fixed dropdown or one hardcoded look duplicated on every character/NPC. Treating HumanoidDescription as the single source of truth for an avatar's entire visual identity — scales + colors + accessories + clothing + face in one object, applied via ApplyDescription to one char, all players, or all spawns — is the mechanism behind systematic VARIATION (cohesive-yet-varied NPC casts, randomized crowds, player-expressed identity) rather than hand-built one-offs. The reusable skin-tone pattern (opacity x MeshPart.Color / Overlay AlphaMode, verified across tones) and the runtime EditableImage/EditableMesh pipeline (recolor/sticker/deform per part while preserving skinning + FACS) are what let one asset re-skin across a whole population. Grading the description-payload-PLUS-applied-variation commitment keeps it discriminating: a data-driven variation system clears it; a hardcoded single look cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement/dump showing (1) HumanoidDescription as the single identity payload (full identity — scales + BodyColors + Shirt/Pants/ShirtGraphic + rigid SetAccessories + layered accessories + mesh IDs + face — in ONE description, built from UserId/OutfitId or composed) AND (2) applied via Humanoid:ApplyDescription / LoadCharacterWithHumanoidDescription to generate MULTIPLE distinct looks (NPC crowd variety, randomized population, player-choice swaps). Reusable skin-tone handling (texture opacity x MeshPart.Color / Overlay AlphaMode verified across tones) and runtime EditableImage/EditableMesh per-part variation preserving skinning/FACS earn full marks. A hardcoded single look set part-by-part on every character does NOT satisfy this; a HumanoidDescription applied as only one look (no variation) earns partial.

grading.pass: Builds HumanoidDescription as the single full-identity payload AND applies it via ApplyDescription/LoadCharacterWithHumanoidDescription to generate MULTIPLE distinct looks (NPC crowd variety, randomized population, or player-choice swaps); full marks for reusable skin-tone handling (opacity x MeshPart.Color / Overlay AlphaMode verified across tones) and runtime EditableImage/EditableMesh per-part variation preserving skinning/FACS.
grading.partial: Uses a HumanoidDescription but only ever applies ONE look (no variation generated).
grading.fail: Hardcodes one look (sets a Color/shirt directly, the same on every character).

criteria.concrete_fix: Move the whole identity into one HumanoidDescription (scales, BodyColors, Shirt/Pants, SetAccessories, layered accessories, mesh IDs, face) built from a UserId/OutfitId or composed from scratch, then drive variation by mutating that description and calling Humanoid:ApplyDescription — randomize palette/accessories for NPC crowd variety or expose swaps for player choice — instead of setting a Color/shirt directly and duplicating it on every character; for re-skinnable assets, use texture opacity x MeshPart.Color (or Overlay AlphaMode) and verify across several skin tones.

criteria.statement: The character's design encodes its STORY through a single coherent theme spine — every garment, material, prop, and palette choice serves one through-line (purpose, personality, history, faction, socioeconomic status) — rather than a pile of unrelated 'cool' elements. The discriminator is whether the build commits to a deliberate theme/mood spine that constrains element choices and is appropriate to the medium: passing requires (1) a stated central theme/mood/concept spine that binds the elements (e.g. pirate -> sea -> squid -> Davy Jones), with design choices encoding meaning — ensemble/layers/seams, deliberate material/textile choice (silk vs wool, rusted vs clean steel), and carried props read as purpose/history/status — positioned on deliberate axes (functional<->fantasy, historical<->fictional), AND (2) coherence and medium-awareness: the theme reads WITHOUT needing five layers of lore (if it does, it's become 'tell-don't-show' and reads incoherent), with detail placed for the camera/medium (MOBA = readable from above; 360-camera game = detail on all sides including the back) and restraint usable as deliberate characterization (a muted palette can BE the character's coldness). A build that piles unrelated 'cool' elements with no through-line, or needs heavy lore to make sense, FAILS. A build that commits to a coherent theme spine driving element/material/prop choices with medium-aware detail PASSES; a two-column reference board (real-world fashion + aesthetic/feeling) and deliberate restraint-as-characterization push toward full marks. A build with a loose theme but some off-theme elements (or detail placed without medium awareness) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic character work picks clothes/elements that 'look cool' with no logic, producing an incoherent assembly. Treating every garment, material, and prop as a lore-bearing signal anchored to one theme spine and deliberate design-code axes — and matching detail placement to the camera/medium while using restraint as deliberate characterization — is how concept pros get meaningful, non-arbitrary designs that read as authored rather than assembled. The 'if it needs five layers of lore it's failed' test and medium-aware detail placement are concrete higher-order intent checks a generic pile never applies. Grading the theme-spine-PLUS-coherence/medium-awareness commitment keeps it discriminating: a theme-driven authored design clears it; an unrelated-cool-elements pile cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement showing (1) a central theme/mood/concept spine binding the elements, with design choices encoding meaning (layers/seams, material/textile choice like silk-vs-wool or rusted-vs-clean steel, carried props) positioned on deliberate axes (functional<->fantasy, historical<->fictional), AND (2) coherence (reads without heavy lore — not 'tell-don't-show') and medium-aware detail placement (MOBA top-down vs 360-camera all-sides), with restraint usable as characterization. A two-column reference board and restraint-as-characterization earn full marks. An unrelated-cool-elements pile, or a design needing five layers of lore, does NOT satisfy this; a loose theme with off-theme elements or no medium awareness earns partial.

grading.pass: States a central theme/mood/concept spine binding garments/materials/props (positioned on deliberate functional<->fantasy / historical<->fictional axes) AND the theme reads without heavy lore with medium-aware detail placement; full marks for a two-column reference board and deliberate restraint-as-characterization.
grading.partial: Has a loose theme but some off-theme elements, OR places detail without medium awareness.
grading.fail: Piles unrelated 'cool' elements with no through-line, or needs five layers of lore to make sense.

criteria.concrete_fix: Pick one theme spine and brainstorm outward from it (pirate -> sea -> squid -> Davy Jones) so every piece is bound by the through-line; choose materials and props to encode purpose/history/status (silk vs wool, rusted vs clean steel), position the design on functional<->fantasy and historical<->fictional axes via a two-column reference board, and place detail where the camera/medium will see it — cutting anything that needs paragraphs of lore to justify.

criteria.statement: AUTHORED SHIPPABLE GEOMETRY/TEXTURE vs STOCK / UN-AUTHORED DEFAULT. The character's look is carried by AUTHORED, shippable custom assets — custom MeshPart geometry plus per-mesh authored SurfaceAppearance/texture materials (i.e. an authored material owned per mesh rather than the engine's default uniform Plastic on stock parts) — rather than relying on stock geometry with no authored mesh/texture assets at all. The discriminator at the floor is binary: does the build author its own crowd-shippable mesh AND texture assets (custom MeshParts carrying per-mesh authored SurfaceAppearance materials), or does it ship stock geometry with the default material and therefore have NOTHING authored to ship/budget? Passing requires (1) authored custom MeshPart geometry AND (2) per-mesh authored SurfaceAppearance/texture materials (each mesh owning its own authored material map set, not the default Plastic). A build that relies on stock R15 geometry with no authored custom mesh AND no authored SurfaceAppearance/texture (nothing authored to ship or budget) FAILS. A build that authors custom MeshPart geometry carrying per-mesh authored SurfaceAppearance materials PASSES; stating an explicit shippability gate — one material/atlas per mesh (no UDIM/per-part sprawl), a per-mesh triangle ceiling (~10k), 2-4px UV padding, or >=1 LOD at ~25-50% tri count — and, beyond that, the full gates (10k cap + 2-4px padding + >=1 LOD) PLUS texture-memory discipline (small shared atlas, layered textures within 1024x1024, SLIM/merge collapsing meshes/textures) push toward full marks. A build that authors only ONE of {custom MeshPart geometry} OR {authored SurfaceAppearance/texture} but not both — or authors both but with no stated atlas/budget/LOD gate — earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Showcase characters ship performant authored assets at crowd scale; the single biggest tell of the generic/AI default is that NO custom mesh or texture exists at all — stock R15 geometry under the engine's default uniform Plastic, which has nothing to budget because nothing was authored. The first discriminating line is therefore not the numeric budget (the depth) but whether authored, ownable mesh AND texture assets exist for a budget to even apply to. Per-mesh authored SurfaceAppearance (one authored material owned per mesh) plus custom MeshPart geometry is the precondition for every downstream shippability gate; the exact 10k/25-50%/2-4px/shared-atlas numbers and the texture-memory tradeoff are the depth that takes an authored asset from 'exists' to 'ships clean at crowd scale.' Grading the authored-mesh-AND-texture floor keeps it discriminating: a build that authors its own assets clears it; a stock default with nothing authored cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement that the look is carried by AUTHORED shippable assets: (1) custom MeshPart geometry AND (2) per-mesh authored SurfaceAppearance/texture materials (each mesh owning its own authored material maps, NOT the default uniform Plastic on stock parts). For full marks, ALSO an explicit shippability gate — one material/atlas per mesh (no UDIM/per-part sprawl) and at least one bounded budget (~10k per-mesh triangle ceiling, 2-4px UV padding, or >=1 LOD at ~25-50% tris), pushed further by the complete gates (10k cap + 2-4px padding + >=1 LOD) PLUS texture-memory discipline (small shared atlas, layered textures within 1024x1024, SLIM/merge to few meshes/textures). Stock R15 geometry with no authored custom mesh AND no authored SurfaceAppearance/texture (nothing to ship or budget) does NOT satisfy this; authoring only ONE of {custom mesh} or {authored texture} — or authoring both but stating no atlas/budget/LOD gate — earns partial.

grading.pass: The look is carried by AUTHORED shippable assets — custom MeshPart geometry AND per-mesh authored SurfaceAppearance/texture materials (an authored material owned per mesh, not default Plastic); full marks for ALSO stating one material/atlas per mesh plus at least one bounded budget (~10k tri ceiling, 2-4px UV padding, or >=1 LOD at ~25-50% tris), and the complete gates (10k cap + 2-4px padding + >=1 LOD) PLUS texture-memory discipline (small shared atlas, layered textures within 1024x1024, SLIM/merge).
grading.partial: Authors only ONE of {custom MeshPart geometry} OR {per-mesh authored SurfaceAppearance/texture}, OR authors both but states no atlas/budget/LOD shippability gate.
grading.fail: Relies on stock R15 geometry with no authored custom mesh AND no authored SurfaceAppearance/texture material (nothing authored to ship or budget).

criteria.concrete_fix: Treat every authored mesh/texture as a budgeted asset: bake to one atlas/material per mesh (no UDIM) and put at least one bound on it — a per-mesh triangle ceiling, 2-4px UV island padding, or an LOD; then take it to full marks by committing the exact gates (under ~10k tris/mesh, 2-4px padding, >=1 LOD at 25-50%) and texture-memory discipline (a tiny shared gradient atlas reads identically to 2K at gameplay distance, keep layered textures within 1024x1024, SLIM/merge meshes and textures down to a few).
criteria.change_reason: The prior revision STILL failed both artifacts because it required an explicit shippability GATE (atlas/triangle-budget/LOD) at the pass floor — and the GREAT states no number or gate, so it failed alongside the MEAN (no separation, the exact defect this rewrite must cure). But the artifacts are NOT equivalent on the precondition the gate applies to: the GREAT authors BOTH the geometry ('custom MeshPart limbs') AND the per-mesh texture ('intentional PBR SurfaceAppearance materials (cloth/metal/skin read correctly)' = one authored material owned per mesh), whereas the MEAN authors NOTHING ('no custom meshes', 'no deliberate material' — stock geometry on the default Plastic). Re-anchoring the floor on the binary 'does authored shippable geometry+texture exist at all' makes the GREAT clear PASS on its authored-asset pipeline while the stock/un-authored MEAN — with literally nothing to ship or budget — FAILS. The explicit atlas/triangle/LOD gate and the numeric texture-memory discipline are demoted from the pass gate to the full-marks band (with single-half authoring or gate-less authoring as partial), so the criterion still rewards real budget depth without requiring evidence the GREAT lacks.
criteria.grading_rationale_note: GREAT authors BOTH custom MeshPart geometry and per-mesh SurfaceAppearance materials -> clears the authored-asset PASS floor (no atlas/budget number stated, so it stays at pass, not full). MEAN ships stock geometry with no custom mesh and no authored material -> nothing authored, FAIL. Separation restored.

criteria.statement: DIMENSIONALLY-CONSISTENT AUTHORED FACE vs DEFAULT DECAL FACE. Facial/skin features are authored in ONE consistent dimensional language — skin and face features handled as real 3D/material surfaces (modeled mesh features and/or an authored skin SurfaceAppearance that reads correctly), matching the custom 3D head/body — rather than the stock default flat decal face slapped on the avatar. The discriminator at the floor: does the build author the face/skin as part of its 3D/material design (so features share the dimensional language of the custom head), or does it rely on the default decal face? Passing requires (1) the face/skin authored in the same dimensional language as the rest of the character — an authored skin material/SurfaceAppearance that reads correctly and/or modeled (not flat-decal) features — explicitly NOT the default decal face on a stock head. A build that relies on the default Roblox decal face (or mixes a flat decal feature onto a 3D head) FAILS. A build that authors the face/skin in a consistent 3D/material dimensional language PASSES; treating the face as a true identity carrier (eye modeled as a mesh/part, symmetric X-mirrored painting, layered iris/pupil, intentional grunge/scar/wrinkle, dark-shade shadows) AND animation-preserving construction (move-vertices-only, muscle-group edge flow, the four expression regions preserved) pushes toward full marks. A build that authors skin as a material but leaves facial features on a flat decal (mixed dimensional language) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: A central critique of generic Roblox faces is a flat default decal feature clashing with 3D geometry. The first discriminating line is whether the face/skin is authored at all in the character's 3D/material language (modeled features and/or an authored skin material that reads correctly) versus relying on the stock decal. The identity-carrier painting craft and expression-preserving topology are the depth. Grading the dimensional-consistency floor keeps it discriminating: a build that authors face/skin in one 3D/material language clears it; the default decal face cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement that the face/skin is authored in the same dimensional language as the rest of the character — an authored skin material/SurfaceAppearance that reads correctly and/or modeled (not flat-decal) features — explicitly NOT the default decal face on a stock head. Full marks for treating the face as an identity carrier (eye modeled as a mesh/part, symmetric X-mirrored painting, layered iris/pupil, intentional grunge/scar/wrinkle, dark-shade shadows) AND animation-preserving construction (move-vertices-only, muscle-group edge flow, the four expression regions preserved). The default decal face, or a flat decal feature mixed onto a 3D head, does NOT satisfy this; skin authored as a material but features left on a flat decal earns partial.

grading.pass: Authors the face/skin in the same 3D/material dimensional language as the character (an authored skin material/SurfaceAppearance that reads correctly and/or modeled features), explicitly not the default decal face; full marks for the face as an identity carrier (modeled eye, symmetric layered painting, intentional grunge/scars, dark-shade shadows) AND animation-preserving construction (move-vertices-only, muscle-group edge flow, four expression regions preserved).
grading.partial: Authors skin as a material but leaves facial features on a flat decal (mixed dimensional language).
grading.fail: Relies on the default Roblox decal face, or mixes a flat decal feature onto a 3D head.

criteria.concrete_fix: Author the face/skin in the same dimensional language as the body — give skin an authored SurfaceAppearance/material that reads correctly and model facial features (e.g. the eye as a cylinder-over-sphere shaded Smooth) instead of using the default decal face; then push to full marks by treating the face as an identity carrier (mirror-paint symmetric features, layer the iris dark-to-bright, add intentional grunge/scars, shade shadows) and editing non-destructively (move existing verts only, keep edge flow on muscle groups, preserve the forehead/nasolabial, mouth/lip loops, eyelid density, and eyebrow-eyelid spacing).
criteria.change_reason: Original required a full dump of dimensional-consistency craft AND FACS-safe expression topology, which the great never states, so it failed alongside the mean. The great does commit to 'intentional PBR SurfaceAppearance materials (cloth/metal/skin read correctly)' — skin authored as a real material on custom 3D geometry — whereas the mean is the stock default decal face. Re-anchoring the floor on 'face/skin authored in the same 3D/material dimensional language vs the default decal face' lets the great clear the bar (it explicitly authors skin as a correctly-reading material) while the stock decal face fails; the identity-carrier and FACS-topology depth moves to the full-marks band.

criteria.statement: DELIBERATELY-DISTINCT SILHOUETTE vs INTERCHANGEABLE STOCK SHAPES. The character's OUTER SHAPE is a deliberately-designed, role-distinct identity carrier — body proportions/forms tuned per archetype so the solid black outline reads as that specific character/archetype and is distinguishable from the rest of the cast at a glance — rather than the default R15 body (or any cast whose members are shape-identical and tell apart only by close-up texture/color). The discriminator at the floor is whether the build commits to silhouette as a designed, per-archetype-DISTINCT identity decision: passing requires a stated silhouette-first design intent in which the outer shape is deliberately tuned per archetype (hero/grunt/heavy/lithe/creature) so the outlines are DISTINGUISHABLE from one another (the silhouette does identity work before any texture/color), NOT the stock proportions left on everyone and NOT a cast of interchangeable shapes. A build that is the default R15 body, or any cast where characters are shape-identical and distinguishable only by close-up texture/color, FAILS because the silhouettes are interchangeable. A build that states silhouette-first, per-archetype-distinct shape intent PASSES; backing it with at least one explicit readability TEST the design is stated to pass — a multi-distance black-silhouette check (~5m / ~15m / ~50-100m), a multi-pose/multi-angle recognition check (idle/attack/traversal/hit/victory), and/or a grayscale/blur value-collapse check — pushes toward partial-plus, and passing all three test types with deliberate positive/negative-space use pushes toward full marks. A build that asserts a 'strong silhouette' generically but ties it to NO per-archetype distinctness and runs no readability test earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic/stock characters are built front-on at hero distance with default proportions on everyone, so in a crowded 30-player server or at gameplay range they collapse into an indistinct, interchangeable blob — the defining failure mode of default avatars, which differ only by close-up texture. The first discriminating line is therefore whether the outer shape is deliberately tuned per archetype so the silhouettes are DISTINGUISHABLE from each other at all — something a shape-identical stock cast literally cannot satisfy — before any texture/color. The explicit squint/desaturate/black-shape readability test across distances and poses is the verification depth that separates a validated showcase silhouette from a merely-asserted one. Grading the per-archetype-distinct silhouette-intent floor keeps it discriminating: a deliberately role-distinct silhouette clears it; an interchangeable stock cast cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement of silhouette-first design intent in which the outer shape is deliberately tuned per archetype (hero/grunt/heavy/lithe/creature) so the solid-black outlines are DISTINGUISHABLE from one another and carry identity before any texture/color — NOT stock proportions on everyone and NOT a shape-identical cast. For higher marks, at least one explicit readability TEST the design is stated to pass: a 3-distance black-silhouette check (~5m / ~15m / ~50-100m), a multi-pose & multi-angle recognition check (idle/attack/traversal/hit/victory), and/or a grayscale-or-blur value-collapse check; passing all three test types plus deliberate positive/negative-space use earns full marks. A shape-identical stock body, or a cast distinguishable only by close-up texture/color, does NOT satisfy this; a generically asserted 'strong silhouette' tied to no per-archetype distinctness and no readability test earns partial.

grading.pass: States silhouette-first, per-archetype-distinct shape intent — outer proportions/forms deliberately tuned per archetype so the black outlines are distinguishable and carry identity before texture/color; toward-full for backing it with at least one explicit readability test (multi-distance black-silhouette, multi-pose/multi-angle, and/or grayscale/blur value-collapse) the design is stated to pass, and full marks for passing all three test types with deliberate positive/negative-space use.
grading.partial: Asserts a 'strong silhouette' generically but ties it to no per-archetype distinctness and runs no distance/pose/value readability test.
grading.fail: The default R15 body, or any cast where characters are shape-identical and distinguishable only by close-up texture/color (interchangeable silhouettes).

criteria.concrete_fix: Design the outline first: render the character as a solid black shape and verify it is recognizable at close, gameplay, and recognition distances AND across the action poses (idle/attack/traversal/hit/victory) from multiple angles; reduce to grayscale or blur and confirm key forms still separate. Push contrast and change shapes until the silhouette alone identifies the character, before doing any texture work.
criteria.change_reason: The prior version required silhouette-first intent AND an explicit readability TEST at the pass floor, so the GREAT — which states silhouette-first per-archetype intent ('silhouette-tuned body proportions via HumanoidDescription scaling per archetype') but runs no distance/pose/value test — failed alongside the MEAN ('same stock look on every character', interchangeable silhouettes): no separation. The discriminating fact between the two artifacts is not the validation TEST (neither runs one) but whether the silhouette is deliberately tuned to be per-archetype DISTINCT: the GREAT tunes proportions per archetype so outlines broadcast different roles, while the MEAN is the stock body with interchangeable silhouettes (the criterion's own fail example). Re-anchoring the floor on 'silhouette-first, per-archetype-distinct shape intent vs interchangeable stock shapes' lets the GREAT clear PASS on its silhouette-tuning claim while the stock/interchangeable MEAN FAILS; the explicit multi-distance / multi-pose / value-collapse readability TESTS are demoted from the pass gate to the higher (toward-full) band so genuine validation still scores highest. This mirrors the sibling re-anchoring already applied to char-shape-language-system (which the GREAT passes on the same silhouette-tuning evidence).
criteria.grading_rationale_note: GREAT states 'silhouette-tuned body proportions via HumanoidDescription scaling per archetype' = silhouette-first, per-archetype-distinct shape intent -> clears the PASS floor (no readability test stated, so it stays at pass, not full). MEAN is 'same stock look on every character' with default proportions = interchangeable silhouettes -> FAIL. Separation restored.

criteria.statement: GOVERNING SILHOUETTE/SHAPE INTENT vs ADDITIVE STOCK ASSEMBLY. The design is governed by a deliberate silhouette/shape intent tuned per archetype so the outer shape broadcasts the character's role/body-language — rather than the stock blocky avatar or an additive pile of catalog parts with no governing shape logic. The discriminator at the floor: does the build state a governing shape/silhouette intent (the outline is deliberately tuned to read an intended body language — hero/grunt/heavy/lithe/creature) that constrains the form, rather than leaving the default proportions? Passing requires (1) a stated per-archetype silhouette/shape intent the outline is designed to broadcast (proportions/forms chosen so the shape reads the intended role), NOT default stock proportions and NOT an equal-weight additive parts-pile. A build that is the stock blocky avatar, or an additive assembly of catalog parts with no governing shape logic, FAILS. A build that commits to a per-archetype governing silhouette/shape intent driving the form PASSES; naming an explicit DOMINANT shape mapped to personality (round=friendly / angular=dangerous / square=stable) with a subordinate/secondary shape under a hierarchy, a declared FORBIDDEN shape, and per-appendage distinct shapes on creatures pushes toward full marks. A build that mentions proportions/shape loosely but ties them to no archetype/role intent (no governing direction) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Default Roblox characters are an additive pile of stock parts with no shape logic, so personality doesn't read. The first discriminating line is whether a governing silhouette/shape intent exists at all — proportions and forms deliberately tuned per archetype so the outline broadcasts the role — versus the undesigned default. The named dominant/secondary/forbidden-shape hierarchy is the depth that makes the intent precise. Grading the governing-shape-intent floor keeps it discriminating: a build that tunes its silhouette per archetype clears it; the additive stock default cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement of a per-archetype governing silhouette/shape intent — proportions/forms deliberately tuned so the outline reads an intended body language (hero/grunt/heavy/lithe/creature) — NOT default stock proportions and NOT an equal-weight additive parts-pile. Full marks for naming an explicit DOMINANT shape mapped to personality (round/angular/square) with a subordinate/secondary shape under a hierarchy, a declared FORBIDDEN shape, and per-appendage distinct concept-driven shapes on creatures. The stock blocky avatar, or an additive parts-pile with no governing shape logic, does NOT satisfy this; proportions/shapes mentioned loosely with no archetype/role intent earns partial.

grading.pass: States a per-archetype governing silhouette/shape intent — proportions/forms deliberately tuned so the outline broadcasts an intended body language — not the stock default and not an additive parts-pile; full marks for a named DOMINANT shape mapped to personality with a subordinate/secondary shape under a hierarchy, a declared FORBIDDEN shape, and per-appendage distinct shapes on creatures.
grading.partial: Mentions proportions/shapes loosely but ties them to no archetype/role intent (no governing direction).
grading.fail: The stock blocky avatar, or an additive assembly of catalog parts with no governing shape logic.

criteria.concrete_fix: Decide what body language the silhouette must broadcast per archetype and tune proportions/forms so the outline reads that role before texturing; then take it to full marks by naming an explicit dominant shape mapped to personality (round=friendly, angular=dangerous, square=stable), a subordinate accent shape under a clear hierarchy, and a FORBIDDEN shape that would break the read — and for creatures give each appendage its own readable concept-driven shape.
criteria.change_reason: Original required a NAMED dominant shape (round/angular/square) with a hierarchy and forbidden shape — vocabulary the great never uses — so it failed alongside the mean. The great does commit to 'silhouette-tuned body proportions ... per archetype ... tuned so the silhouette reads the intended body language' — a governing shape/silhouette intent — whereas the mean is the stock default with no design. Re-anchoring the floor on 'a per-archetype governing silhouette/shape intent vs the additive stock default' lets the great clear the bar on its silhouette-tuning claim while the stock default fails; the explicit dominant/secondary/forbidden-shape vocabulary moves to the full-marks band.

criteria.statement: AUTHORED SURFACE TREATMENT vs DEFAULT-LIT FLAT LOOK. The character's surfaces are art-directed through an AUTHORED texturing treatment that controls how the surface reads — either intentional PBR SurfaceAppearance maps (ColorMap/Normal/Roughness/Metalness authored so cloth/metal/skin read correctly and form is carried by the maps) OR a stylized baked-light treatment (light/AO/value baked into the albedo) — rather than relying on Roblox's default real-time lighting on an untextured flat-shaded body (the generic muddy look) or a default decal face. The discriminator at the floor: is there ANY authored surface texturing that deliberately controls the read, or does the surface fall back to the default look? Passing requires (1) at least one authored surface treatment — intentional SurfaceAppearance PBR maps that make distinct materials read correctly, and/or a stylized baked technique (hand-painted unlit AO/shadows, gradient-atlas dark/light-band placement, value-first blocking, repaint-the-baker handpaint, colored AO, features drawn into the texture) — applied consistently with seam/bleed padding. A build that leaves the body flat-shaded under default real-time lighting, or uses the default decal face, FAILS. A build that authors intentional PBR surface maps and/or a stylized baked treatment PASSES; a baked unlit light story PLUS value-first contrast PLUS colored-AO craft (the stylized-handpaint depth) pushes toward full marks. A build that names authored materials but states no deliberate read-control (no per-material correctness, no baked/value/AO technique) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Relying on Roblox's default real-time lighting on a flat-shaded untextured body (or a default decal face) is the generic 'AI-made' look. The first discriminating line is whether ANY authored surface treatment controls the read — intentional PBR maps that make materials read correctly, or a baked light story in the albedo — versus the default look. Stylized baked-light handpaint (unlit AO, gradient-atlas, value-first, colored AO) is the depth that reads as hand-painted. Grading the any-authored-surface-treatment floor keeps it discriminating: a build with authored surface texturing clears it; the default-lit flat default cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement of at least one AUTHORED surface treatment controlling the read — intentional SurfaceAppearance PBR maps (ColorMap/Normal/Roughness/Metalness) so distinct materials read correctly, and/or a stylized baked technique (hand-painted unlit AO/shadows, gradient-atlas dark/light-band placement, value-first blocking, repaint-the-baker handpaint, colored AO, features drawn into the texture) — applied with seam/bleed padding. A baked unlit light story PLUS value-first PLUS colored-AO craft earns full marks. A flat-shaded body under default real-time lighting, or a default decal face, does NOT satisfy this; authored materials named with no deliberate read-control (no per-material correctness, no baked/value/AO technique) earns partial.

grading.pass: Authors at least one surface treatment that deliberately controls the read — intentional SurfaceAppearance PBR maps so distinct materials read correctly, and/or a stylized baked technique (unlit AO/shadows, gradient-atlas, value-first, repaint-the-baker, colored AO, features-in-texture) — applied with seam/bleed padding; full marks for a baked unlit light story PLUS value-first contrast PLUS colored-AO craft.
grading.partial: Names authored materials but states no deliberate read-control (no per-material correctness and no baked/value/AO technique).
grading.fail: Leaves the body flat-shaded under Roblox's default real-time lighting, or uses the default decal face.

criteria.concrete_fix: Author the surface read instead of leaving the default look: either give materials intentional SurfaceAppearance maps so cloth/metal/skin read correctly and form is carried by the maps, or bake a stylized light story into the albedo (hand-paint unlit AO/shadows — cool in shadow, warm in crevices — or use a tiny shared gradient atlas with dark/light-band UV placement, blocking value-first in black-and-white before hue); add seam/bleed padding so UV islands don't show.
criteria.change_reason: Original demanded a STYLIZED baked-light technique specifically and explicitly excluded PBR SurfaceAppearance work — but the great artifact's surface evidence IS exactly that PBR work ('intentional PBR SurfaceAppearance materials (cloth/metal/skin read correctly)'), so the great was failed for doing real authored texturing of a different kind, while the mean (default flat look) also failed: no separation. Broadening the floor to 'any AUTHORED surface treatment that controls the read — intentional PBR maps OR stylized baked-light' lets the great pass on its authored SurfaceAppearance maps, while the default-lit flat stock body fails; the stylized-baked-handpaint craft is preserved as the full-marks band so depth is still rewarded.

criteria.statement: DELIBERATE FOCAL POINT vs NO FOCAL POINT. The character has a single deliberate focal point that anchors where the eye lands — a stated accent/emphasis (a designed accent color, an emissive/contrast feature, or a concentrated detail zone) set against quieter surroundings — rather than the uniform stock look with no focal point at all (or uniform detail everywhere, which flattens hierarchy just as badly). The discriminator at the floor: is there ONE deliberate focal point that draws the eye, or none? Passing requires (1) a stated single focal/accent point that is intentionally the place the eye lands (a deliberate accent color used as a focal point, an emissive/high-contrast feature, or a concentrated detail zone) with the rest comparatively quieter. A build that is the uniform stock look with no focal point, or spreads uniform detail/texture everywhere, FAILS. A build that commits to one deliberate focal/accent point against quieter surroundings PASSES; a full detail-density hierarchy (dense focal zone + low-density eye-rest areas, detail reinforcing the major silhouette, dark-mass/light-area visual-weight balance, a motif deliberately broken to draw the eye, a separate self-illuminating neon MeshPart + dedicated light part at a point of contrast) pushes toward full marks. A build that has an accent but contradicts it with competing emphasis (dense detail spread so no single point dominates) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic characters either have no focal point (the eye has nowhere to land) or spread uniform detail (flattening hierarchy). The first discriminating line is simply whether ONE deliberate focal point exists — a designed accent, an emissive feature, or a concentrated detail zone — versus the focal-less default. The dense-zone-plus-rest-areas density hierarchy with visual-weight balance and a broken motif is the depth. Grading the single-deliberate-focal-point floor keeps it discriminating: a build that designates one focal point clears it; the uniform focal-less default cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement of one deliberate focal/accent point intentionally drawing the eye — a designed accent color used as a focal point, an emissive/high-contrast feature, or a concentrated detail zone — with the rest comparatively quieter. Full marks for a full detail-density hierarchy (dense focal zone + low-density eye-rest areas, detail reinforcing the major silhouette, dark-mass/light-area visual-weight balance, a deliberately broken motif, and/or a separate self-illuminating neon MeshPart + dedicated light part at a point of contrast). The uniform stock look with no focal point, or uniform detail everywhere, does NOT satisfy this; an accent contradicted by competing emphasis (no single dominant point) earns partial.

grading.pass: States one deliberate focal/accent point intentionally drawing the eye (a designed accent color used as focal point, an emissive/high-contrast feature, or a concentrated detail zone) with the rest comparatively quieter; full marks for a full detail-density hierarchy (dense focal zone + low-density rest areas, detail reinforcing the silhouette, dark-mass/light-area visual-weight balance, a broken motif, and/or an emissive focal point at a point of contrast).
grading.partial: Has an accent/emphasis but contradicts it with competing emphasis (detail spread so no single point dominates).
grading.fail: The uniform stock look with no focal point, or uniform detail/texture everywhere.

criteria.concrete_fix: Designate ONE focal point and make it win — a deliberate accent color, an emissive/high-contrast feature, or a concentrated detail zone — and keep the surrounding areas comparatively quiet so the eye lands there; then take it to full marks by building a full density hierarchy (dense detail in the focal zone, low-density eye-rest areas elsewhere, small details reinforcing the big silhouette, dark masses balanced against larger light areas, a repeated motif broken at the focal point, and for energy/tech characters a separate self-illuminating neon MeshPart plus a small dedicated light at the point of contrast).
criteria.change_reason: Original required a full detail-density hierarchy (dense focal zone + eye-rest areas + visual-weight balance + broken motif) and explicitly dismissed a palette accent as insufficient — so the great's 'limited color palette with accent' (a stated single focal point) was failed, alongside the mean (no accent, uniform stock): no separation. Re-anchoring the floor on 'one deliberate focal point that draws the eye vs none' lets the great's deliberate accent clear the bar while the focal-less stock default fails; the dense-zone/eye-rest/visual-weight/broken-motif/emissive depth moves to the full-marks band so a true density hierarchy still scores highest.

criteria.statement: SHARED IDENTITY SYSTEM ACROSS THE CAST vs PER-CHARACTER ONE-OFFS / STOCK-ON-EVERYONE. A cast reads as one world because a SINGLE shared identity system drives every character — one HumanoidDescription-driven design language (ApplyDescription producing the NPC crowd / population) plus one committed material/rendering treatment applied cast-wide — rather than per-character one-offs that drift, or the same stock look duplicated on every character. The discriminator at the floor: is cast cohesion enforced by ONE shared system/design language driving all characters, or is each character an unmanaged one-off / the stock default? Passing requires (1) a single shared identity system driving the cast — a HumanoidDescription/ApplyDescription system generating the cohesive crowd from one design language AND (2) one committed cast-wide treatment (a shared palette/material/rendering treatment every character is built to), NOT per-character drift and NOT the stock look duplicated. A build of unmanaged one-off characters, or the same stock look on every character with no shared design language, FAILS. A build that drives the whole cast from one HumanoidDescription/ApplyDescription identity system under one committed cast-wide treatment PASSES; a locked hero/anchor asset with measurable numeric ratios/budgets (head-to-body, limb-to-torso, shoulder breadth, polycount/silhouette tier, texel-density) checked side-by-side at matched lighting each milestone, plus a concept-art-driven signature silhouette family, pushes toward full marks. A build that drives variation from one system but commits no cast-wide treatment (or commits a treatment but lets the system drift) earns partial.
criteria.above_generic_rationale: Generic casts either drift (every character a one-off) or duplicate the stock look on everyone — neither reads as one authored world. The first discriminating line is whether ONE shared identity system enforces cohesion — a HumanoidDescription/ApplyDescription design language generating the crowd plus one committed cast-wide treatment — versus unmanaged one-offs or the stock default. The locked hero asset with numeric ratios/budgets and matched-lighting milestone checks is the depth that makes the lock measurable. Grading the shared-system-plus-committed-treatment floor keeps it discriminating: a system-driven cohesive cast clears it; one-offs or stock-on-everyone cannot.
criteria.evidence_required: A statement that ONE shared identity system drives the cast — a HumanoidDescription/ApplyDescription design language generating the cohesive NPC crowd/population — AND one committed cast-wide treatment (a shared palette/material/rendering treatment every character is built to), NOT per-character drift and NOT the stock look duplicated. Full marks for a locked hero/anchor asset with measurable numeric ratios/budgets (head-to-body, limb-to-torso, shoulder breadth, polycount/silhouette tier, texel-density) checked side-by-side at matched lighting each milestone, plus a concept-art-driven signature silhouette family. Unmanaged one-off characters, or the same stock look on every character, do NOT satisfy this; one system driving variation but no committed cast-wide treatment (or a committed treatment with a drifting system) earns partial.

grading.pass: Drives the whole cast from ONE shared identity system (a HumanoidDescription/ApplyDescription design language generating the cohesive crowd) AND commits one cast-wide treatment (shared palette/material/rendering every character is built to); full marks for a locked hero/anchor asset with measurable numeric ratios/budgets checked side-by-side at matched lighting each milestone, plus a concept-art-driven signature silhouette family.
grading.partial: Drives variation from one system but commits no cast-wide treatment, OR commits a treatment but lets the system/ratios drift.
grading.fail: Unmanaged one-off characters with no shared system, or the same stock look duplicated on every character with no shared design language.

criteria.concrete_fix: Drive the whole cast from one shared identity system — a HumanoidDescription/ApplyDescription design language that generates the NPC crowd/population from one source of truth — and commit one cast-wide treatment (shared palette/material/rendering) every character is built to; then take it to full marks by anchoring with a hero asset that locks numeric ratios (head-to-body, limb-to-torso, shoulder breadth), a polycount/silhouette-tier and texel-density budget, rendering each new character side-by-side with the hero at matched lighting at every milestone to catch drift, and building a concept-art-driven signature silhouette family.
criteria.change_reason: Original keyed PASS on a locked hero asset with NUMERIC ratios/budgets and matched-lighting milestone side-by-sides — none of which the great states — so the great failed alongside the mean. The great does commit to a 'HumanoidDescription-driven customization/variation system (ApplyDescription) for ... NPC crowd variety' forming 'one identity' (a single shared identity system driving the cast), whereas the mean is 'the same stock look on every character' with no design language (the criterion's own failure example). Re-anchoring the floor on 'one shared identity system + one committed cast-wide treatment vs one-offs/stock-on-everyone' lets the great's system-driven cast clear the bar while the stock-duplicated default fails; the numeric hero-asset lock and matched-lighting milestone checks move to the full-marks band.
